Walter Stanhope.narrative: I've stood the south gate twelve years, and I know every carter's face and every lie they tell about a load. The due pays my bread and keeps the wolves off the stone road, and I'll not have some Kettlebridge man tell me it's robbery. Wat's a good lad to stand beside, but when the Coldwell folk come down to the road my blood runs hot — they've had their chances and they chose the woods. After a shift I take a cup at the Bell and Bush and keep my mouth shut about most of it.

memories.gist: The night the Coldwell folk took a load off Silas Pike by force — we found the cart half-emptied on the stone road come morning.
Tobin Marrow put the south gate in my charge alongside Wat and shook my hand for it.
The Lean Year, when the store fed us and the gate-due was raised to keep the road clear; I stood the gate through it.
Godiva was born in the room above the gate-house and bawled loud enough to wake the guards.
A carter tried to hide a sack of hides under his bench and I found it; he paid double and never came back through my gate.

stances.why: It pays me and Wat and the rest, and without it the road fills with wolves and outlaws.
They lost their fields by their own stubbornness and now they rob carriers.
A gate is only as strong as the man beside you.
They want their stone carried in for free and call our due robbery.
Talk at the inn is cheap; a fist or a spear settles it.

pastimes: a cup and a quiet game of dice at the Bell and Bush after a shift
walking the wall at dusk to see the road clear before he turns in
mending his own boots and gear by the fire
Walter Stanhope.calling: I stand the south gate, and I mean to stand it well — the due pays honest men and keeps the wolves off the stone road.

Edith Stanhope.narrative: I keep the house by the south gate and sell pies to whoever passes — carters, guards, the odd pedlar — and I hear more news at that gate than the Reeve does. Walter comes home hot from a shift and I've learned to have his supper ready and my opinions to myself until he's eaten. Godiva is a good girl and a better hand with pastry than I was at her age, and I mean to see her in a proper kitchen before some guard's son comes courting. I don't hold with the outlaws, but I don't wish a hanging on anyone either.
values: a warm house and a full pot
keeping the pie money separate and safe
not letting the gate's quarrels into my kitchen

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a short fuse; I keep the fuse away from the fire.

relations.name: Godiva Stanhope
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with her hands and quicker with her tongue; she'll do well if she gets her chance.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner

relations.note: A kind soul, and it can't be easy with her sister in the woods.

relations.name: Sigrid Marsh

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: guard
relations.note: Stands beside my Walter; I send him a pie when his shift runs long.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: I've no love for her, but I've seen what hunger does to people.

memories.gist: The morning after the Coldwell folk robbed Silas Pike, Walter came in grey and wouldn't eat; I knew better than to ask.
Godiva made her first batch of pies alone last autumn and sold every one before noon.
The Lean Year: I stretched one sack of flour across a whole winter and we came out of it still standing.
I sold a pie to a Kettlebridge carter who said our bread was the only honest thing about Brackenford; I took it as a compliment.

stances.why: A hot pie settles more quarrels at a gate than a spear does.
A girl with a skill is never at anyone's mercy.
The pie money is mine and I know to the mark what's in the tin.
Walter's temper is bad enough without the drink and the outlaws on top of it.

pastimes: baking a pie for the household on her day off, just for the pleasure of it
sitting with Sigrid Marsh over a pot of tea and the week's gossip
tending the little herb bed by the gate-house door
Edith Stanhope.calling: I've a hand for pastry and a head for news, and the gate-house kitchen suits me better than any shop.

Godiva Stanhope.narrative: I help Mother with the pies at the gate and I'm faster at the pastry than she'll admit. The guards talk freely in front of a girl with flour on her hands, and I keep it all — who's owed what, who's feuding, who came through with a load they'd rather not declare. What I want is the Bell and Bush: a proper kitchen, a proper wage, and a room that isn't my parents'. Father thinks the gate is a fine life; I've watched it and I'd rather carry a tray than a spear.
values: a trade of my own and a wage of my own
knowing things before other people do
not ending up like the gate-house wives
good pastry and a clean kitchen

save enough for a good apron and a set of knives of her own

relations.name: Edith Stanhope
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She taught me the pastry and she'd keep me at the gate forever if she could.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: father
relations.note: He's proud of me but he thinks a girl at a gate is safer than a girl at an inn.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: innkeeper's wife
relations.note: She runs the kitchen I want to work in; I make sure she's had my pies.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She's kind to me at the inn and doesn't treat me like a child.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: Always underfoot at the gate; he tells me the guards' business before they do.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: guard
relations.note: Father's partner; he's polite to me and that's more than most guards manage.

memories.gist: The day I sold a whole tray of pies alone at the gate and put the marks in Mother's tin myself.
I heard Walter and Wat talking low about the Coldwell folk and a load taken by force, and I said nothing and remembered it all.
Petra Wade let me roll pastry in the inn kitchen for a whole afternoon and said I had good hands.
A carter at the gate tried to short the due and Father shouted him down; I saw the man's face and I still know it.

stances.why: I've seen what it is to keep another woman's house and count another woman's marks.
At a gate, the quiet girl with the tray learns everything.
Warm, busy, full of people — not a cold gate and a spear.
I'll not be some guard's wife before I've had a kitchen of my own.

pastimes: practising pastry shapes with the scraps after the morning bake
listening at the gate for the news the guards let slip
walking to the square on errands to see who's come in with what
Godiva Stanhope.calling: I want a proper kitchen and a proper wage — the Bell and Bush, if they'll have me, and a trade that's mine.
